claims.text: The starting material is as-received, pre-exposure Q235 mild steel.
The controlled intervention anneals Q235 at 750 °C in an oxygen-rich atmosphere for 1, 5, or 10 hours.
Oxygen-rich annealing of Q235 at 750 °C produces a coherent and adherent surface oxide layer.
The annealing-generated oxide layer consists of magnetite and/or hematite.
The proposed hot-corrosion exposure uses a mixture of 75% Na2SO4 and 25% NaCl at 700–900 °C.
Parallel room-temperature tests in a neutral electrolyte are proposed for comparison with hot-corrosion behavior.
A continuous and adherent annealing-generated iron oxide scale acts as a barrier that limits further corrosion.
The annealing-generated iron oxide scale is self-healing under high-temperature hot-corrosion conditions.
Enhanced oxidation kinetics at high temperature enable rapid healing of the oxide film.
At room temperature, the oxide is too thin and static to provide significant corrosion protection.
Pre-oxidized Q235 will exhibit less mass loss during high-temperature molten-salt exposure than untreated Q235.
Pre-oxidized Q235 will exhibit fewer oxide-spallation events during high-temperature molten-salt exposure than untreated Q235.
Pre-oxidized and untreated Q235 will show only minimal corrosion-performance differences at room temperature.
Untreated Q235 does not develop a significant protective oxide layer under the tested conditions.
The proposed protective mechanism applies predominantly in high-temperature molten-salt environments where oxide formation and healing are kinetically active.
The proposed protective mechanism does not significantly affect corrosion at ambient temperature because oxidation activity is limited.
Failure to observe a coherent, self-healing scale together with significantly lower mass loss and spallation in pre-oxidized samples would falsify the proposed mechanism.
